prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in time and frequency measurement.

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks fit the discovery-or-invention criterion cleanly. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between many atoms and Doppler or recoil shifts, and the subsequent realization, especially in Ye's strontium clocks, took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. The invention is concrete and independently reproduced in several laboratories. It already underpins tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy, and it is the leading route to a redefinition of the second. Attribution is the most compact on the shortlist: two names, a clear conceptual originator and a clear performance leader. Opening support is broad, with five top-three placements and two first places. I moved it above my own opening first choice for that reason. B014 and B005 both have strong cross-committee support, and B005 has the cleaner credit and a longer record of independent confirmation.
statement.case_against: The area sits next to the frequency-comb prize (2005) and the ion-control prize (2012), so the committee may judge it incremental on recognized ground. The practical payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. Priority among early lattice-clock proposals and demonstrations, and the role of the strongest ion-clock competitors, are not settled by the supplied names, and a two-name prize leaves other groups out. B014 has a wider effect on condensed-matter physics and a cleaner theory-plus-experiment story that may outrank a measurement-science advance.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are a clear original invention, and the open question is whether lattice clocks should be grouped with ultrastable-laser or frequency-comb work, which would change the allocation.
responses.response: I agree on the merit but would keep the citation specific to the lattice clock. The comb was recognized in 2005, and the ultrastable cavity lasers are an enabling technology whose names are not on this ballot. Widening the citation would blur attribution and push the prize past three people. The magic-wavelength concept and its realization to 1e-18 is the discovery-or-invention in question, and it can be stated without crediting the whole clock ecosystem.

responses.point: Twisted bilayer graphene is a clean pairing of MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, with Bistritzer a junior contributor, and the lattice clock overlaps earlier prizes in subject area.
responses.response: Your two-name version of B014 is a fair way to keep the theory-plus-experiment story inside a tidy configuration, and I take the point seriously because the 2011 continuum model credits Bistritzer and MacDonald jointly. I would not drop the person who co-authored the decisive prediction on seniority alone. On overlap, I disagree that the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the clock redundant. Those prizes recognized the comb and single-quantum-system control. The lattice clock is a distinct invention that those tools made possible and did not already contain.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opens moire quantum matter, but the mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states remain unsettled.
responses.response: I share your enthusiasm for B014, and it is my second choice. My reservation is maturity. Seven years after the 2018 experiments the field is very active but the central physical question, why the superconductivity appears, is open, and sample variability, strain and disorder still matter. A clock at 1e-18 has been reproduced by several groups and its systematics are understood. If the committee prefers a field-defining discovery despite unresolved mechanism, I could support B014, but I would want that stated openly in the citation.

responses.point: The optical lattice clock is the best frequency standard ever built, but practical redefinition of the second has not occurred, so impact is partly prospective.
responses.response: That is fair, and it is my main hesitation about a prize that rests partly on future use. I think the criterion is the demonstrated performance and the already realized scientific use in constants tests and geodesy, and not a formal redefinition, which is an institutional process. I would also note that your first choice, B035, rests on the diffuse flux discovery with source identification still incomplete, so on maturity the two are not far apart. I find B005's attribution more compact.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether priority among early magic-wavelength proposals and first lattice-clock demonstrations changes the two-name credit.
Whether B014 should outrank B005 given its larger field-wide effect, and how much weight the unresolved superconducting mechanism deserves.
statement.conflict_note: My opening first choice was B051 (aberration-corrected electron optics), which is close to my own field of transmission electron microscopy and to the community I lead internationally. I have not placed it first here to avoid a self-interested preference, and I would step back from deciding on it. I have no specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer apparent from my profile. Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson has no apparent link to B005 or B014 in the profile.
